title: Why We Built Meetily When Every Meeting Tool Already Existed | Meetily Blog

children.text: Why We Built Meetily When Every Meeting Tool Already Existed
A client told us they weren't comfortable with a bot in the meeting. We looked for a tool that kept the audio on our own machines, found none, and built one.

children.alt: Cover reading Why We Built Meetily - a note from our CEO - with first commit December 2024, no bot joining the call, on-device by default, and MIT open source

children.text: A client told us they weren't comfortable with a bot in the meeting. Every tool we looked at uploaded the audio to its own servers, so we built one that didn't, used it internally, and pushed it to GitHub on December 26, 2024. Meetily transcribes meetings on your own device by default, with nothing joining the call.
A client said it plainly: "I'm not comfortable with a bot in this meeting."

We were on a call - a strategy discussion, the kind where real decisions get made - and they stopped us before we could hit record. They knew our meeting assistant was there. They knew what it did. And they'd decided that whatever convenience it offered wasn't worth what it cost them: a cloud server somewhere holding a recording of this conversation.
We thought about it. They were right.

We'd been using an AI notetaker for months. It saved time, caught things we'd miss, generated summaries we actually read. But here's what the privacy policy said, summarized plainly: your audio goes to our servers, we process it there, and you trust us with what happens next. We'd clicked through that policy without reading it carefully. Our client had read it.

That week, we looked for an alternative. We looked hard. Every tool we found operated on the same architecture: record on your device, upload to their cloud, process on their servers, store there unless you ask otherwise. The transcription quality varied. The pricing varied. The privacy story was identical.

That wasn't a startup decision. It was a practical one. We're a software company — we build things for clients. Building a tool for internal use is part of what we do. The goal was simple: keep the audio on our machines, get the summaries, never upload anything anywhere. We didn't need it to be beautiful. We needed it to work.

The first version was rough, macOS only, required more patience to set up than we'd like to admit, and occasionally unreliable. But when we used it in client meetings, we could answer the question - where does my data go? - with one word: nowhere.
Then we made a decision that changed everything. We open-sourced it.

Not because we planned to build a company. We did it because we asked ourselves: is this our problem, or is it everyone's problem? We looked at the market. We looked at the privacy lawsuits accumulating against meeting tools - class actions, biometric data suits, institutional bans. We looked at the companies who couldn't use any of these tools because their compliance teams said no. We decided this was everyone's problem.
We pushed the first commit to GitHub on December 26, 2024. Within weeks, the stars came in.

A year after that first commit, we sold Meetily Pro to our first enterprise clients. December 2025. The year between was not a smooth product launch - it was a listening exercise. We built speaker diarization because users needed to distinguish voices in recorded conversations. We rebuilt onboarding because the people who needed this most weren't developers comfortable with a technical setup. We rethought what customer support meant when users were trusting us with something sensitive.

By February 2026, 10,000 people had starred the repository. Feature requests came from developers in Europe, enterprise teams in the US, small businesses in Asia. People weren't just asking for improvements - they were telling us the same story our client had told us: I can't trust these tools with my data, and I've been waiting for something different.
People ask why we built Meetily when so many meeting tools already existed.

The honest answer: we didn't build it to compete. We built it because a client trusted us enough to say they were uncomfortable, and we took that seriously. The tools that existed had made a choice - convenience over control, cloud processing over local privacy - and they'd made it for their users, not with them. We made a different choice.

The principle hasn't changed since that first rough prototype: your meetings belong to you. Your audio stays on your machine, unless you choose otherwise. We bring you the power of AI. We don't need your data to do it.
That's not a feature. It's the reason we exist.

children.a: Meetily is an open-source AI meeting assistant built by Zackriya Solutions. It records and transcribes meetings on your own device instead of uploading the audio to a vendor's servers, and it does it without anything joining the call - it captures your system audio, so it works with Zoom, Teams, Meet, Discord, or any other app that produces sound. The code is on GitHub under the MIT license, and the Community Edition is free.

Zackriya Solutions, a software company, first built it for internal use. A client said they were not comfortable with a bot in the meeting, and every tool available at the time uploaded meeting audio to its own servers. We built something that kept the audio on our own machines, used it in client meetings, and then open-sourced it. The first commit went to GitHub on December 26, 2024.

children.q: Does Meetily use a meeting bot?
children.a: No. Meetily captures audio from your own device, so nothing joins the call as a participant. There is no extra attendee in the list and nothing to admit from the waiting room.

children.q: Where does my meeting audio go?
children.a: By default it stays on your machine. Transcription runs on your device and recordings are stored there. Meetily Pro also offers an opt-in cloud transcription option; if you switch that on, the audio goes to the provider you chose, under your own account. For summaries you pick the model - a local one, or your own API key, in which case only the transcript text goes to that provider under their terms. None of it routes through Zackriya Solutions.

The Community Edition is free and open source under the MIT license. Pro is $10/user/month billed annually and adds features, not a different transcription engine - every edition runs the same one. Enterprise pricing is custom.

children.q: What platforms does Meetily run on today?
children.a: Windows and macOS have native desktop apps. The very first version in early 2025 was macOS only; Windows arrived shortly after. There is no native Linux build today.

children.alt: Under the EU AI Act, a meeting tool's risk depends on how you use it: summarizing calls is not high-risk, scoring employees is high-risk from December 2027, reading emotions at work is banned since February 2025, and EN 18286 is the first standard

children.text: Your Meeting Tool's Risk Level Under the EU AI Act Isn't Set by the Vendor. It's Set by You.
The EU AI Act's four risk categories cover uses, not products. The same meeting tool can be low-risk, high-risk or banned. Plus the 2027 timeline and EN 18286.
